messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mara, a 28‑year‑old European police officer, was 45 minutes into a night patrol when the call that would change her life came in. A 23‑year‑old man had been found in a parked car with a weapon, and the squad had already been dispatched. Mara arrived to find the suspect unresponsive, and another officer had already fired a warning shot into the air. The shot rang out, the sound a harsh, metallic clang that seemed to reverberate into Mara’s bones. The man did not die immediately, but he was later pronounced dead, and a coroner ruled the fatal shot had come from the other officer’s gun. The scene left Mara shaking; her hands had clenched around her radio as she watched the suspect’s body go still. She felt a pang of betrayal—someone she had sworn to protect had, in a split second, turned weapon against a fellow officer. In the weeks that followed, the memory of that night did not stay buried. Whenever the hum of a police radio or the distant echo of a siren rose, Mara found herself transported back to the fluorescent glare of the victim’s empty chest and the crack of gunfire. The recollection was not a distant flash; the sights, the sharp, acrid smell of gunpowder, the trembling of the suspect’s hands—it all flooded her senses simultaneously, as if the scene were happening again. Yet the memory felt oddly foreign, as though it belonged to another person, and she could not tell when she was looking at it and when it was looking at her. It burst into her mind at the most inconvenient times, forcing her to stare at the ceiling or to clutch her chest until the pulse in her ears subsided. She could not control when it would surface, and each intrusion felt as if it were a separate entity, a ghost of a night that was neither hers nor wholly remote. Mara’s body had come to respond as though danger were ever present. Even when she sat on the front bench of a grocery store, her shoulders tense, her heart racing, she could not shake the feeling that someone was watching. She started to believe that the world itself was hostile, that danger could erupt from any stranger’s face. The betrayal she felt at the time of the shooting amplified these fears; she was convinced that someone she had trusted had turned on her. The conviction that the world was dangerous made her hyper‑vigilant: a sudden shout from a passing cyclist would feel like a threat, a shadow in the parking lot a possible attacker. Her negative appraisals, therefore, set the stage for her memories to intrude. In any setting where a siren wailed or a bright flash startled her, her mind could not resist the lure of the night’s trauma. The belief that danger lurked in the ordinary became a trigger that pulled the intrusive memory out of its hidden place and into her present consciousness. This loop of appraisals and memory intrusions tightened the longer she avoided confronting the experience. The intrusive memories, in turn, reinforced Mara’s negative appraisals. Each time the image of the gunshot re‑ignited, her heart hammered, her muscles tensed, and she felt her world shrink to a single point of potential threat. She began to think that she was no longer safe even in the most mundane places. The memory’s full sensory fidelity—seeing the man’s pale face, hearing the crack of the gun, feeling the cold air of the station—made her believe that the same scene could repeat itself. She started to doubt her own judgment: “If I can’t trust my senses to tell me I’m safe, how can I trust my body?” The memory thus kept the sense of danger alive, and she became convinced that betrayal had once again taken root in her life. When the pattern of avoidance grew, the impact on her job and her personal life became undeniable. Mara began arriving late to shifts, hoping to avoid any situation that might bring the memory to the surface. Her partner began to notice her growing reluctance to engage in patrol duties, and the couple she shared a home with expressed concern over the increasing distance between them. Her supervisor requested that she attend a safety training session on stress management, but Mara declined, fearing that the discussion would trigger her memories and prove her world still as dangerous as ever. The sense that the world was hostile made her doubt whether she could ever be at peace, both at work and at home. Today, Mara is finally seeking help because each day she wakes with a pulse racing, unable to focus on her own children’s homework or on the hum of the city outside her window. She fears that she will lose her job, lose the trust of those she loves, and that the memory will keep haunting her until she can no longer hold her job as a police officer. She hopes that by facing the trauma she can regain control of her body’s reactions, feel safe again in her everyday life, and reconcile the betrayal she experienced with the role she loves.
